nameStory: The thread-leaved sundew gets its name from its incredibly thin, thread-like leaves that look almost like green fishing line. The 'sundew' part comes from the sparkling dewdrops that always seem to cover the leaves - though these aren't actually dew at all, but sticky traps! These glistening droplets catch the morning light like tiny diamonds, giving the plant its beautiful common name.
description: Thread-leaved sundew is a fascinating carnivorous plant that looks like a tiny green fountain sprouting from boggy ground. Its long, thin leaves grow straight up like green threads, each one covered in what looks like morning dew but is actually sticky glue for catching insects. The whole plant is quite small, rarely getting taller than 8-10 inches, and forms a neat little rosette at the base. In summer, it sends up delicate pink or purple flowers on tall, slender stalks that tower above the trapping leaves.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, thin, thread-like leaves that stand straight up and unroll in spirals like tiny fern fiddleheads. Each leaf is covered in hundreds of tiny, clear, sticky droplets that feel tacky to the touch and often have small insects stuck to them.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a small rosette at ground level with leaves emerging from the center and standing erect like thin green needles. The whole plant looks like a miniature green fountain or sea anemone.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink or purple flowers bloom on tall, thin stalks that rise well above the leaves in summer. Flowers open one at a time along the stalk, starting from the bottom.

idTips.label: Sticky Traps
idTips.description: Every leaf is covered in clear, glistening droplets that never dry up, even in bright sun. These feel sticky like honey and often have tiny gnats, flies, or other small insects stuck to them.

habitat: Found in acidic, nutrient-poor bogs, wet sandy areas, and the edges of cranberry bogs throughout New England. Look for it in constantly moist, peaty soils where the ground stays soggy year-round, often growing alongside sphagnum moss, pitcher plants, and other bog specialists. It thrives in full sun locations where few other plants can survive the harsh, acidic conditions.

seasonality.spring: New leaves begin unfurling in spirals from the center of the plant, looking like tiny green corkscrews. The sticky droplets become more prominent as the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for identification - leaves are fully extended and covered in glistening droplets, often with trapped insects visible. Pink or purple flowers bloom on tall stalks above the leaves.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to turn reddish and may start to die back. Seeds ripen and are released from small capsules along the flower stalks.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in northern areas, though the root system remains alive underground. In milder areas, some leaves may persist but appear dormant.

funFact: This tiny plant is such an efficient insect-catching machine that scientists have found over 200 small flies and gnats stuck to a single plant! The sticky droplets work like natural flypaper, and the plant actually digests its prey to get nutrients that are missing from the nutrient-poor bog soil.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with very young pine seedlings from a distance, but the sticky droplets and lack of woody stem immediately give it away. No other New England plant has this combination of thread-like upright leaves covered in permanent sticky dewdrops.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sundew,' the glistening droplets aren't dew at all but a specially produced sticky substance called mucilage that the plant manufactures to trap insects. This is one of nature's most efficient carnivorous plant traps, working 24 hours a day regardless of weather conditions.
compareHints: Unlike its sundew relatives, thread-leaved sundew has long, thin, upright leaves rather than the round, flat leaves of round-leaved sundew or the spoon-shaped leaves of spoonleaf sundew. The thread-leaved variety also grows much taller and more upright, while the other sundews hug the ground with their leaves spread horizontally. All three species share the characteristic sticky droplets, but only thread-leaved sundew has leaves that unroll in spirals like fern fiddleheads.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Round-leaved sundew differs from spoonleaf sundew by its perfectly circular leaves (versus oval spoon-shaped ones) and typically grows in more open bog areas.
Spoonleaf sundew differs from round-leaved sundew by its spoon-shaped leaves (versus perfectly round) and its tendency to grow in wetter areas.
